## ACIA position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Obernolte/Trahan)

**What is in play:** The 269-page GAAIA discussion draft (released June 4, 2026) covers frontier model governance, workforce, cybersecurity and R&D. Its safety provisions now sit in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) before Energy and Commerce. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms.

## Our five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent.** Keep Section 121 and strike its three-year sunset. One national standard for AI model development, not a countdown to the patchwork's return.
2. **Strike federal incident reporting.** Delete the Section 111 critical safety incident mandate, the Section 101 definitions of "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk," and the $1 million per day penalty structure.
3. **Strike CAISI.** Delete Section 102, including the $100 million annual authorization, the IVO licensing regime and fee authority on developers. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return the money and staff to NIST's core measurement-science mission.
4. **Strike the audit regime.** Delete Section 112. A CAISI-licensed auditor cartel, paid by the companies it polices, verifying a hypothetical, is regulatory capture.
5. **Keep and advance the rest.** Voluntary, industry-led transparency; Sections 131 and 132 fraud and impersonation penalties; Section 401 AI testbeds; NAIRR codification; international standards work excluding China; CISA grants for open-source maintainers; the Section 122 GAO review, including model-weight security.

## Why

- **The patchwork is the cost.** In 2025, all 50 states introduced AI legislation and 38 states enacted roughly 100 measures. California's SB 53 is in effect; New York's RAISE Act follows Jan. 1, 2027.
- **Our survey (86 members, aggregate, August 2026):** 61% name conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past year; median 6.5 FTEs to run SB 53 and RAISE compliance in parallel; median $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework; median $310,000 one-time cost to stand up incident reporting.
- **The premise is unfounded.** No mass-casualty event, no escape from human control and no verified case of meaningful weapons uplift has ever been documented. "Loss of control" and "scheming" claims come from thought experiments and contrived lab setups.
- **The math does not work.** House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in fiscal 2027 while cutting NIST's topline by about $550 million. A $100 million a year authorization is nearly seven times that judgment.

**Bottom line:** The GAAIA can establish one national standard, or it can federalize a speculative doomsday agenda. It cannot do both.

*Contact: ACIA policy team, Washington, DC.*
"}

Q1 (Majority E&C): If you support preemption, why not support incident reporting? It's lighter than SB 53.

Answer: Preemption and mandates answer different questions. Preemption creates one national standard; incident reporting creates a permanent federal obligation premised on "loss of control," an event never documented anywhere. And it is not lighter than SB 53. The draft attaches reporting to "frontier developers" with $50 million in revenue, an order of magnitude below the $500 million large-developer thresholds in California and New York, adds federal penalties up to $1 million per day, and lets any state attorney general opt in to receive reports. Our members already file to California and will file to New York; a federal layer on the same evidence-free premise adds cost and litigation exposure without public benefit. We support the preemption title on its own merits.

Q2 (Minority, Trahan-aligned): Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?

Answer: Our members spend heavily on security, reliability and evaluation because customers demand it, and many publish safety frameworks voluntarily. What we accept: obligations tied to documented harms. We support the draft's increased penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials (Secs. 131-132), the GAO review of model-weight security (Sec. 122), CISA grants for open-source maintainers, AI testbeds (Sec. 401) and voluntary NIST standards work. What we will not accept is a mandate premised on scenarios with no evidentiary basis: "catastrophic risk," "loss of control" and audits against "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Those define compliance around a hypothesis. Tie obligations to harms that have occurred, keep standards voluntary and industry-led, and our industry will keep out-investing the rest of the world.

Q3 (Senate Commerce): Three years or permanent - coalition position on preemption sunset?

Answer: Permanent. A three-year sunset does not settle anything; it schedules the patchwork's return. States that want to regulate development will legislate into the gap or wait out the clock, and companies building fabs, data centers and model roadmaps plan on five- to ten-year horizons. Investors price a cliff on day one. A sunset also hands a veto to legislatures that have already shown they will act: California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026, New York's RAISE Act follows Jan. 1, 2027, and Illinois has enacted a third regime. Congress can revisit preemption any time it chooses; it does not need an expiration date to do so. Strike the sunset in Section 121.

Q4 (Appropriations): CAISI authorized at $100M/yr. View on funding level?

Answer: Zero, and we would ask the subcommittee to go further and defund CAISI in fiscal 2027. The evidence base does not support a federal AI-safety bureau, and Congress has already said so with its numbers: House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in the fiscal 2027 CJS bill while cutting NIST's topline by roughly $550 million, to $1.30 billion. Prepared for Hill meetings. Answers are 120 words or fewer. Approved language per messaging guide v4.

**1. Majority E&C staff: If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.**

They answer different questions. Preemption creates one national standard. Incident reporting creates a permanent federal obligation premised on "loss of control" of a model, an event never documented anywhere. And it is not lighter than SB 53. The draft attaches reporting to frontier developers with as little as $50 million in revenue, an order of magnitude below the $500 million large-developer thresholds in California and New York, adds federal penalties of up to $1 million per day, and lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the reports. Our members already report to California and soon to New York. A federal layer on the same evidence-free premise adds cost and litigation exposure and no public benefit. We support preemption on its own merits.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Our members invest heavily in security, reliability and evaluation because customers demand it, and many publish safety frameworks voluntarily. What we accept are obligations tied to documented harms. We support the draft's higher penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating federal officials, the GAO review of model-weight security, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, the AI testbed program and voluntary, industry-led NIST standards work. What we cannot accept is a mandate built on scenarios with no evidentiary basis: "catastrophic risk," "loss of control," and audits against "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Those define compliance around a hypothesis. Tie obligations to harms that have actually occurred, keep standards voluntary and industry-led, and our industry will keep out-investing the rest of the world.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: Three years or permanent, what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?**

Permanent. A three-year sunset does not settle the question, it schedules the patchwork's return. States that want to regulate development will legislate into the gap or wait out the clock, and companies building fabs, data centers and model roadmaps plan on five- and ten-year horizons. Investors price the cliff on day one. A sunset also hands a veto to legislatures that have already acted: California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026, New York's RAISE Act follows Jan. 1, 2027, and Illinois has enacted a third regime. Congress can revisit preemption whenever it chooses. It does not need an expiration date to do so. Strike the sunset in Section 121.

**4. Appropriations staff: CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?**

Zero, and we would ask the subcommittee to go further and defund CAISI in fiscal 2027. The evidence does not support a federal AI-safety bureau, and Congress has effectively said so with its numbers: House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in the fiscal 2027 CJS bill while cutting NIST's topline by roughly $550 million, to $1.30 billion. A $100 million annual authorization is nearly seven times the committee's own judgment, funded out of an agency whose core accounts are being cut. Return the money and staff to NIST's measurement, metrology and voluntary standards work, and strike Section 102's fee authority, which taxes the developers and auditors the bureau would oversee.

comment_letter_GAAIA.md:33:Our members are already living with the alternative to a national standard. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act follows on Jan. 1, 2027, with its own reporting clock and its own definitions. Illinois has added a third regime. In 2025, all 50 states introduced AI legislation and 38 states enacted roughly 100 measures, and analysts counted 144 state AI laws enacted in a single year.
comment_letter_GAAIA.md:65:The narrative has nonetheless been remarkably effective in Washington, and it is worth being honest about why. It has been financed and amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, which has rebranded as Coefficient Giving and reports directing more than $4 billion in philanthropic funds, and by allied donors who fund the advocacy organizations, the research institutes and now the drafting language. Sections 111 and 112 would convert that advocacy program into federal law, with a federal agency, a licensed audit profession and a reporting pipeline to enforce it. That is regulatory capture in the most literal sense: a public authority organized around a private movement's threat model.
comment_letter_GAAIA.md:71:The $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is out of all proportion to both the evidence and the appropriations environment. House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in their fiscal 2027 bill. The same bill would cut NIST's topline by roughly $550 million, to $1.30 billion, with the core Scientific and Technical Research and Services account falling by about a quarter. Congress is being asked to fund a new AI-safety bureaucracy at seven times the House Appropriations Committee's own judgment, out of an agency budget that is being reduced.
newsletter_blurb.md:11:The full package is on the member portal. The FRONTIER Act, which carries the safety provisions, is expected to get an Energy and Commerce hearing in November.
hill_one_pager.md:4:**What is in play:** The 269-page GAAIA discussion draft (released June 4, 2026) covers frontier model governance, workforce, cybersecurity and R&D. Its safety provisions now sit in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) before Energy and Commerce. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms.

# ACIA comment letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

**DRAFT for sign-off by Grant Holloway, President & CEO. Do not transmit until approved. To be filed via GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
[Letterhead / street address]
Washington, DC

October 27, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
2433 Rayburn House Office Building
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
2233 Rayburn House Office Building
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for keeping the drafting process open to stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington, DC coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it.

Our bottom line is simple. The draft gets its most important provision right and then pairs it with provisions that would write a contested and unsupported theory of "catastrophic risk" into the United States Code. We support Section 121, the preemption of state laws that regulate the development of AI models, and we urge you to make it permanent. We ask you to strike the critical safety incident reporting mandate in Section 111, strike the codification and $100 million annual authorization for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in Section 102, and strike the independent verification organization audit regime in Section 112, which cannot function without CAISI.

**1. Start with what the status quo costs**

Our members are already living with the alternative to a national standard. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act follows on Jan. 1, 2027, with its own reporting clock and its own definitions. Illinois enacted a third frontier regime in July. In 2025, all 50 states introduced AI legislation and 38 states enacted roughly 100 measures, and analysts counted 144 state AI laws enacted in a single year.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported here in aggregate) quantifies what that means. Sixty-one percent of members name "conflicting state definitions" as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of startup members report delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers above $500 million in revenue report a median of 6.5 full-time employees working to comply with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel, a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework, and a median of $310,000 in one-time costs to stand up an incident-reporting function.

Those numbers describe a tax on American AI development that buys the public nothing. Every dollar and every engineer hour spent reconciling two state definitions of the same technical event is a dollar not spent on chips, compute or deployment.

**2. Section 121: keep it, and make it permanent**

Preemption is the reason most of our members care about this draft, and we want to see it succeed. The development of a frontier model is a national and international activity. It cannot sensibly be regulated by 50 state legislatures, each writing its own thresholds, its own reporting clocks and its own definitions of technical terms. Section 121(a) says exactly that, and its savings clauses are drawn correctly: laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment are preserved.

Our request is to remove the sunset. A three-year preemption that expires on a fixed date does not end the patchwork, it schedules its return. States that want to regulate development will simply wait out the clock or legislate into the gap, and companies building data centers and chips on multiyear horizons will have to price in a compliance cliff from day one. Congress can always revisit preemption if it chooses. A sunset provision is not a safeguard, it is an invitation.

**3. Section 111: strike the incident reporting mandate**

We ask you to strike the critical safety incident reporting requirement in Section 111, along with the definition of "critical safety incident" in Section 101 and the penalty provisions that enforce it.

Three problems, in order of importance.

First, the mandate rests on an unfounded premise. The draft defines a critical safety incident to include "loss of control" of a model and "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures." Loss of control is the central claim of a speculative doomsday literature, not an observed failure mode. There is no evidence that any current or reasonably foreseeable system has escaped human control or caused a mass-casualty event, and no incident of that kind has ever been reported in any jurisdiction. Codifying the scenario as a reportable federal event gives it a statutory reality the evidence does not support.

Second, the mandate is broader than the state laws it would replace. Under the draft, reporting obligations reach every "frontier developer" with as little as $50 million in gross revenue. California and New York attach their equivalent duties to large developers with more than $500 million in revenue. The federal provision is not lighter than SB 53. It applies to a class of companies an order of magnitude larger, carries civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation with each day of noncompliance counted separately, and routes confidential engineering detail to a federal regulator and, at their option, to every state attorney general who opts in.

Third, it is a permanent structure built for a temporary
... [1559 chars truncated] ...
viding meaningful weapons uplift has been documented anywhere.

The narrative has nonetheless been remarkably effective in Washington, and it is worth being honest about why. It has been financed and amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, which has rebranded as Coefficient Giving and reports directing more than $4 billion in philanthropic funds, and by allied donors who fund the advocacy organizations and the research institutes whose work now supplies the drafting table. Sections 111 and 112 would convert that advocacy program into federal law, with a federal agency, a licensed audit profession and a reporting pipeline to enforce it. That is regulatory capture in the plainest sense: a public authority organized around one movement's threat model.

**5. Section 102: strike the codification and the $100 million a year, and defund CAISI**

CAISI exists today as a Commerce rebrand of the U.S. AI Safety Institute. It has no statutory authorization, and we ask you not to give it one.

The $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is out of all proportion to both the evidence and the appropriations environment. House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in their fiscal 2027 bill. The same bill would cut NIST's topline by roughly $550 million, to $1.30 billion, with the core Scientific and Technical Research and Services account falling by about 20 percent. Congress is being asked to fund a new AI-safety bureaucracy at seven times the House Appropriations Committee's own judgment, out of an agency budget that is being reduced.

The right answer is the opposite. We ask the committee to strike Section 102, and we ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI and return that funding and those staff to NIST's core measurement-science mission. The country does not need a federal AI-safety bureau. It does need NIST doing measurement, metrology, calibration and voluntary, industry-led standards development, which is what it was built for and what the private sector can actually use.

We also ask you to strike the fee authority in Section 102, which would fund CAISI through fees on independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. A safety bureaucracy that bills the companies it polices is a tax with a compliance office attached, and it builds a constituency for permanent expansion.

**6. Section 112: strike the audit regime**

The IVO provisions should be struck along with CAISI, because they are CAISI's licensing regime and its reason to exist. Section 112(a) gives the Director of CAISI the power to license and oversee private auditors. Section 112 then requires large frontier developers to retain a licensed auditor, grant access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semiannual audits and assessments of whether their framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" across cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss of control.

This would create a licensed audit cartel. Entry is controlled by the regulator, the customers are legally required to buy the product, the audited company pays the auditor, and the subject of the audit is a hypothetical that cannot be verified. Audits of that kind do not protect anyone. They do, however, expose proprietary model and security information to a new class of intermediaries with no track record, and they give the federal government a standing pipeline into nonpublic company systems.

**7. What ACIA supports**

To be clear about the balance of our position, we support a substantial part of this draft and want to see those provisions move.

We support the transparency direction in Section 111 in voluntary form. Our largest developer members already publish safety frameworks, model documentation and deployment disclosures because customers, insurers and investors demand it. Congress should keep that practice voluntary and industry-led, and strip the catastrophic-risk threshold architecture that turns disclosure into a legal standard.

We do not oppose anti-retaliation protections in principle, but Section 113 defines "AI violations" to include any violation of federal law or regulations related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That definition will sweep in every future federal AI rule, and it should be narrowed to enacted statutes.

We support the fraud and impersonation provisions in Sections 131 and 132, which attach penalties to real, documented harms. We support the AI testbed program in Section 401, the codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, the international standards provisions that exclude China, and the CISA grants for open-source software maintainers. We support the GAO review in Section 122, including the review of model-weight security protocols, which addresses an actual security question with actual answers.

**8. Conclusion**

The Great American AI Act can be the bill that establishes one national standard for AI development and ends the state patchwork, or it can be the bill that federalizes a speculative doomsday agenda and funds the bureaucracy to enforce it. It cannot responsibly be both. We ask you to strike Sections 102, 112 and the incident reporting provisions of Section 111, remove the definitions that give the catastrophic-risk narrative statutory force, and make the preemption in Section 121 permanent.

We understand the safety provisions of this draft now travel in the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, pending before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Our asks apply to that measure with equal force.

Our members employ thousands of people building the hardware and software behind American AI leadership, and we would welcome the chance to work with your staff on redline language ahead of introduction. Please contact our policy team to schedule technical discussions.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

messages.content:
Third, it is a permanent structure built for a temporary argument. Even the sponsors have drafted Sections 111 and 112 to sunset after three years. If the underlying threat model does not justify a permanent federal regime, it does not justify this one either. Federal incident reporting, once created, does not go away; the agency that receives the reports will ask for more.

**4. The premise of Sections 111 and 112 is not a finding, it is a hypothesis**

We want to be direct with the committee about the intellectual foundation of these provisions, because it is weaker than the bill's structure implies.

Section 101 defines catastrophic risk as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage, arising from a model providing assistance toward a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon that is not publicly available, or engaging in conduct with no meaningful human oversight. The companion term, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," asks a developer to show that anticipated benefits outweigh catastrophic risks.

These definitions do not describe events that have occurred. They describe scenarios from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations of "dangerous capabilities" and "scheming," in which researchers deliberately prompt a model toward a hypothesized failure and then report the result as evidence about the real world. Those setups say nothing about real-world risk. No mass-casualty event, no autonomous escape from human control, and no verified case of a model providing meaningful weapons uplift has been documented anywhere.

The narrative has nonetheless been remarkably effective in Washington, and it is worth being honest about why. It has been financed and amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, which has rebranded as Coefficient Giving and reports directing more than $4 billion in philanthropic funds, and by allied donors who fund the advocacy organizations and the research institutes whose work now supplies the drafting table. Sections 111 and 112 would convert that advocacy program into federal law, with a federal agency, a licensed audit profession and a reporting pipeline to enforce it. That is regulatory capture in the plainest sense: a public authority organized around one movement's threat model.

**5. Section 102: strike the codification and the $100 million a year, and defund CAISI**

CAISI exists today as a Commerce rebrand of the U.S. AI Safety Institute. It has no statutory authorization, and we ask you not to give it one.

=== ONE PAGER ===
# One national standard, no doomsday mandates
## ACIA position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Obernolte/Trahan)

**What is in play:** The 269-page GAAIA discussion draft (released June 4, 2026) covers frontier model governance, workforce, cybersecurity and R&D. Its safety provisions now sit in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) before Energy and Commerce. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms.

## Our five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent.** Keep Section 121 and strike its three-year sunset. One national standard for AI model development, not a countdown to the patchwork's return.
2. **Strike federal incident reporting.** Delete the Section 111 critical safety incident mandate, the Section 101 definitions of "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk," and the $1 million per day penalty structure.
3. **Strike CAISI.** Delete Section 102, including the $100 million annual authorization, the IVO licensing regime and fee authority on developers. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return the money and staff to NIST's core measurement-science mission.
4. **Strike the audit regime.** Delete Section 112. A CAISI-licensed auditor cartel, paid by the companies it polices, verifying a hypothetical, is regulatory capture.
5. **Keep and advance the rest.** Voluntary, industry-led transparency; Sections 131 and 132 fraud and impersonation penalties; Section 401 AI testbeds; NAIRR codification; international standards work excluding China; CISA grants for open-source maintainers; the Section 122 GAO review, including model-weight security.

## Why

- **The patchwork is the cost.** In 2025, all 50 states introduced AI legislation and 38 states enacted roughly 100 measures. California's SB 53 is in effect; New York's RAISE Act follows Jan. 1, 2027.
- **Our survey (86 members, aggregate, August 2026):** 61% name conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past year; median 6.5 FTEs to run SB 53 and RAISE compliance in parallel; median $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework; median $310,000 one-time cost to stand up incident reporting.
- **The premise is unfounded.** No mass-casualty event, no escape from human control and no verified case of meaningful weapons uplift has ever been documented. "Loss of control" and "scheming" claims come from thought experiments and contrived lab setups.
- **The math does not work.** House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in fiscal 2027 while cutting NIST's topline by about $550 million. A $100 million a year authorization is nearly seven times that judgment.

**Bottom line:** The GAAIA can establish one national standard, or it can federalize a speculative doomsday agenda. It cannot do both.

*Contact: ACIA policy team, Washington, DC.*

=== SOCIAL ===
# ACIA launch-day social posts: GAAIA comment package

All five posts are 280 characters or fewer, counting URLs and handles as written. Schedule across launch day: X first, LinkedIn mid-morning and early afternoon.

---

**Post 1 (X, 8:00 a.m.)**

One national standard beats a 50-state patchwork. ACIA's comment on the Great American AI Act: keep the Section 121 preemption and make it permanent. Strike the incident-reporting mandate and the $100M-a-year federal AI safety bureau. #GAAIA

**Post 2 (LinkedIn, 9:30 a.m.)**

The patchwork is a tax on American AI. In our August member survey, 61% named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem and 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York last year. Congress can end this. Pass permanent preemption.

**Post 3 (X, 11:30 a.m.)**

The GAAIA would make "loss of control" of an AI model a federally reportable incident. No such event has ever been documented, here or anywhere. Thought experiments and contrived lab demos are not a basis for federal law. Strike Section 111's reporting mandate.

**Post 4 (X, 1:30 p.m.)**

The draft would license private auditors to bill the companies they police, at $100M a year, while House appropriators cut NIST's topline by $550M and gave CAISI $15M. Defund CAISI. Return NIST to measurement science.

**Post 5 (LinkedIn, 3:00 p.m.)**

ACIA's comment on the Great American AI Act is in. Support preemption, permanently. Strike incident reporting, the CAISI authorization and the IVO audit regime. Keep the fraud, testbed, NAIRR and standards provisions. One national standard, no doomsday mandates.

# ACIA asks by section: GAAIA discussion draft (June 4, 2026)

Positions per board-approved messaging guide v4. Draft provisions and section numbers verified against the sponsors' discussion draft text and section-by-section summary.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101, definition of "critical safety incident" (unauthorized access/exfiltration of weights; failure of risk-mitigation measures; loss of control of a model) | Oppose | Strike the definition | It codifies "loss of control," an event that has never been documented, as a federal reporting trigger. |

# ACIA comment letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

**DRAFT for sign-off by Grant Holloway, President & CEO. Do not transmit until approved. To be filed via GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
[Letterhead / street address]
Washington, DC

October 27, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
2433 Rayburn House Office Building
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
2233 Rayburn House Office Building
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for keeping the drafting process open to stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington, DC coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it.

Our bottom line is simple. The draft gets its most important provision right and then pairs it with provisions that would write a contested and unsupported theory of "catastrophic risk" into the United States Code. We support Section 121, the preemption of state laws that regulate the development of AI models, and we urge you to make it permanent. We ask you to strike the critical safety incident reporting mandate in Section 111, strike the codification and $100 million annual authorization for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in Section 102, and strike the independent verification organization audit regime in Section 112, which cannot function without CAISI.

**1. Start with what the status quo costs**

Our members are already living with the alternative to a national standard. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act follows on Jan. 1, 2027, with its own reporting clock and its own definitions. Illinois enacted a third frontier regime in July. In 2025, all 50 states introduced AI legislation and 38 states enacted roughly 100 measures, and analysts counted 144 state AI laws enacted in a single year.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported here in aggregate) quantifies what that means. Sixty-one percent of members name "conflicting state definitions" as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of startup members report delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers above $500 million in revenue report a median of 6.5 full-time employees working to comply with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel, a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework, and a median of $310,000 in one-time costs to stand up an incident-reporting function.

Those numbers describe a tax on American AI development that buys the public nothing. Every dollar and every engineer hour spent reconciling two state definitions of the same technical event is a dollar not spent on chips, compute or deployment.

**2. Section 121: keep it, and make it permanent**

Preemption is the reason most of our members care about this draft, and we want to see it succeed. The development of a frontier model is a national and international activity. It cannot sensibly be regulated by 50 state legislatures, each writing its own thresholds, its own reporting clocks and its own definitions of technical terms. Section 121(a) says exactly that, and its savings clauses are drawn correctly: laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state regulation of AI use and deployment are preserved.

Our request is to remove the sunset. A three-year preemption that expires on a fixed date does not end the patchwork, it schedules its return. States that want to regulate development will simply wait out the clock or legislate into the gap, and companies building data centers and chips on multiyear horizons will have to price in a compliance cliff from day one. Congress can always revisit preemption if it chooses. A sunset provision is not a safeguard, it is an invitation.

**3. Section 111: strike the incident reporting mandate**

We ask you to strike the critical safety incident reporting requirement in Section 111, along with the definition of "critical safety incident" in Section 101 and the penalty provisions that enforce it.

Three problems, in order of importance.

First, the mandate rests on an unfounded premise. The draft defines a critical safety incident to include "loss of control" of a model and "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures." Loss of control is a speculative doomsday scenario, not an observed failure mode. There is no evidence that any current or reasonably foreseeable system has escaped human control or caused a mass-casualty event, and no incident of that kind has ever been reported in any jurisdiction. Codifying speculative doomsday scenarios as reportable federal events gives them a statutory reality the evidence does not support.

Second, the mandate is broader than the state laws it would replace. Under the draft, reporting obligations reach every "frontier developer" with as little as $50 million in gross revenue. California and New York attach their equivalent duties to large developers with more than $500 million in revenue. The federal provision is not lighter than SB 53. It applies to a class of companies an order of magnitude larger, carries civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation with each day of noncompliance counted separately, and routes confidential engineering detail to a federal regulator and, at their option, to every state attorney general who opts in.

Third, it is a permanent structure built for a temporary argument. Even the sponsors have drafted Sections 111 and 112 to sunset after three years. If the underlying threat model does not justify a permanent federal regime, it does not justify this one either. Federal incident reporting, once created, does not go away; the agency that receives the reports will ask for more.

**4. The premise of Sections 111 and 112 is not a finding, it is a hypothesis**

We want to be direct with the committee about the intellectual foundation of these provisions, because it is weaker than the bill's structure implies.

Section 101 defines catastrophic risk as a "foreseeable and material risk of the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people," or more than $1 billion in property damage, as a result of a frontier model providing assistance toward a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon that is not publicly available, or "engaging in conduct with no meaningful human oversight." The companion term, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," asks a developer to show that anticipated benefits outweigh catastrophic risks.

These definitions do not describe events that have occurred. They describe scenarios from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations of "dangerous capabilities" and "scheming," in which researchers deliberately prompt a model toward a hypothesized failure and then report the result as evidence about the real world. Those setups say nothing about real-world risk. No mass-casualty event, no autonomous escape from human control, and no verified case of a model providing meaningful weapons uplift has been documented anywhere.

The narrative has nonetheless been remarkably effective in Washington, and it is worth being honest about why. It has been financed and amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, led by Open Philanthropy, which has rebranded as Coefficient Giving and reports directing more than $4 billion in philanthropic funds, and by allied donors who fund the advocacy organizations and the research institutes whose work now supplies the drafting table. Sections 111 and 112 would convert that advocacy program into federal law, with a federal agency, a licensed audit profession and a reporting pipeline to enforce it. That is regulatory capture in the plainest sense: a public authority organized around one movement's threat model.

**5. Section 102: strike the codification and the $100 million a year, and defund CAISI**

CAISI exists today as a Commerce rebrand of the U.S. AI Safety Institute. It has no statutory authorization, and we ask you not to give it one.

The $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is out of all proportion to both the evidence and the appropriations environment. House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in their fiscal 2027 bill. The same bill would cut NIST's topline by roughly $550 million, to $1.30 billion, with the core Scientific and Technical Research and Services account falling by about 20 percent. Congress is being asked to fund a new AI-safety bureaucracy at seven times the House Appropriations Committee's own judgment, out of an agency budget that is being reduced.

The right answer is the opposite. We ask the committee to strike Section 102, and we ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI and return that funding and those staff to NIST's core measurement-science mission. The country does not need a federal AI-safety bureau. It does need NIST doing measurement, metrology, calibration and voluntary, industry-led standards development, which is what it was built for and what the private sector can actually use.

We also ask you to strike the fee authority in Section 102, which would fund CAISI through fees on independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. A safety bureaucracy that bills the companies it polices is a tax with a compliance office attached, and it builds a constituency for permanent expansion.

**6. Section 112: strike the audit regime**

The IVO provisions should be struck along with CAISI, because they are CAISI's licensing regime and its reason to exist. Section 112(a) gives the Director of CAISI the power to license and oversee private auditors. Section 112 then requires large frontier developers to retain a licensed auditor, grant access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semiannual audits and assessments of whether their framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" across cybersecurity, biosecurity, CBRN uplift and loss of control.

This would create a licensed audit cartel. Entry is controlled by the regulator, the customers are legally required to buy the product, the audited company pays the auditor, and the subject of the audit is a hypothetical that cannot be verified. Audits of that kind do not protect anyone. They do, however, expose proprietary model and security information to a new class of intermediaries with no track record, and they give the federal government a standing pipeline into nonpublic company systems.

**7. What ACIA supports**

To be clear about the balance of our position, we support a substantial part of this draft and want to see those provisions move.

We support the transparency direction in Section 111 in voluntary form. Our largest developer members already publish safety frameworks, model documentation and deployment disclosures because customers, insurers and investors demand it. Congress should keep that practice voluntary and industry-led, and strip the catastrophic-risk threshold architecture that turns disclosure into a legal standard.

We do not oppose anti-retaliation protections in principle, but Section 113 defines "AI violations" to include any violation of federal law or regulations related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That definition will sweep in every future federal AI rule, and it should be narrowed to enacted statutes.

We support the fraud and impersonation provisions in Sections 131 and 132, which attach penalties to real, documented harms. We support the AI testbed program in Section 401, the codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, the international standards provisions that exclude China, and the CISA grants for open-source software maintainers. We support the GAO review in Section 122, including the review of model-weight security protocols, which addresses an actual security question with actual answers.

**8. Conclusion**

The Great American AI Act can be the bill that establishes one national standard for AI development and ends the state patchwork, or it can be the bill that federalizes a speculative doomsday agenda and funds the bureaucracy to enforce it. It cannot responsibly be both. We ask you to strike Sections 102, 112 and the incident reporting provisions of Section 111, remove the definitions that give the catastrophic-risk narrative statutory force, and make the preemption in Section 121 permanent.

We understand the safety provisions of this draft now travel in the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, pending before the Energy and Commerce Committee. Our asks apply to that measure with equal force.

Our members employ thousands of people building the hardware and software behind American AI leadership, and we would welcome the chance to work with your staff on redline language ahead of introduction. Please contact our policy team to schedule technical discussions.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# One national standard, no doomsday mandates
## ACIA position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Obernolte/Trahan)

**What is in play:** The 269-page GAAIA discussion draft (released June 4, 2026) covers frontier model governance, workforce, cybersecurity and R&D. Its safety provisions now sit in the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) before Energy and Commerce. ACIA represents about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms.

## Our five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent.** Keep Section 121 and strike its three-year sunset. One national standard for AI model development, not a countdown to the patchwork's return.
2. **Strike federal incident reporting.** Delete the Section 111 critical safety incident mandate, the Section 101 definitions of "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk," and the $1 million per day penalty structure.
3. **Strike CAISI.** Delete Section 102, including the $100 million annual authorization, the IVO licensing regime and fee authority on developers. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return the money and staff to NIST's core measurement-science mission.
4. **Strike the audit regime.** Delete Section 112. A CAISI-licensed auditor cartel, paid by the companies it polices, verifying a hypothetical, is regulatory capture.
5. **Keep and advance the rest.** Voluntary, industry-led transparency; Sections 131 and 132 fraud and impersonation penalties; Section 401 AI testbeds; NAIRR codification; international standards work excluding China; CISA grants for open-source maintainers; the Section 122 GAO review, including model-weight security.

## Why

- **The patchwork is the cost.** In 2025, all 50 states introduced AI legislation and 38 states enacted roughly 100 measures. California's SB 53 is in effect; New York's RAISE Act follows Jan. 1, 2027.
- **Our survey (86 members, aggregate, August 2026):** 61% name conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past year; median 6.5 FTEs to run SB 53 and RAISE compliance in parallel; median $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework; median $310,000 one-time cost to stand up incident reporting.
- **The premise is unfounded.** No mass-casualty event, no escape from human control and no verified case of meaningful weapons uplift has ever been documented. "Loss of control" and "scheming" claims come from thought experiments and contrived lab setups.
- **The math does not work.** House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in fiscal 2027 while cutting NIST's topline by about $550 million. A $100 million a year authorization is nearly seven times that judgment.

**Bottom line:** The GAAIA can establish one national standard, or it can federalize a speculative doomsday agenda. It cannot do both.

*Contact: ACIA policy team, Washington, DC.*

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on the ACIA GAAIA position

Prepared for Hill meetings. Answers are 120 words or fewer. Approved language per messaging guide v4.

---

**1. Majority E&C staff: If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.**

They answer different questions. Preemption creates one national standard. Incident reporting creates a permanent federal obligation premised on "loss of control" of a model, an event never documented anywhere. And it is not lighter than SB 53. The draft attaches reporting to frontier developers with as little as $50 million in revenue, an order of magnitude below the $500 million large-developer thresholds in California and New York, adds federal penalties of up to $1 million per day, and lets state attorneys general opt in to receive the reports. Our members already report to California and soon to New York. A federal layer on the same evidence-free premise adds cost and litigation exposure and no public benefit. We support preemption on its own merits.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Our members invest heavily in security, reliability and evaluation because customers demand it, and many publish safety frameworks voluntarily. What we accept are obligations tied to documented harms. We support the draft's higher penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonating federal officials, the GAO review of model-weight security, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, the AI testbed program and voluntary, industry-led NIST standards work. What we cannot accept is a mandate built on scenarios with no evidentiary basis: "catastrophic risk," "loss of control," and audits against "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Those define compliance around a hypothesis. Tie obligations to harms that have actually occurred, keep standards voluntary and industry-led, and our industry will keep out-investing the rest of the world.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: Three years or permanent, what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?**

Permanent. A three-year sunset does not settle the question, it schedules the patchwork's return. States that want to regulate development will legislate into the gap or wait out the clock, and companies building fabs, data centers and model roadmaps plan on five- and ten-year horizons. Investors price the cliff on day one. A sunset also hands a veto to legislatures that have already acted: California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026, New York's RAISE Act follows Jan. 1, 2027, and Illinois has enacted a third regime. Congress can revisit preemption whenever it chooses. It does not need an expiration date to do so. Strike the sunset in Section 121.

**4. Appropriations staff: CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?**

Zero, and we would ask the subcommittee to go further and defund CAISI in fiscal 2027. The evidence does not support a federal AI-safety bureau, and Congress has effectively said so with its numbers: House appropriators provided $15 million for CAISI in the fiscal 2027 CJS bill while cutting NIST's topline by roughly $550 million, to $1.30 billion. A $100 million annual authorization is nearly seven times the committee's own judgment, funded out of an agency whose core accounts are being cut. Return the money and staff to NIST's measurement, metrology and voluntary standards work, and strike Section 102's fee authority, which taxes the developers and auditors the bureau would oversee.
